title: HTTP Fundamentals
summary: HTTP's request/response model, methods and idempotency, status codes, statelessness, and the headers that matter — the vocabulary every other web topic assumes.

slides.markdown:
HTTP is deliberately simple: a client sends a **request**, the server sends back exactly one **response**. No server-initiated pushes, no persistent conversation state built into the protocol itself — every exchange is its own self-contained round trip.

![HTTP client sending a request and server sending a response](assets/http-request-response.svg)

That simplicity is a feature: it's why HTTP scaled to become the web's universal protocol — any client and any server that both speak HTTP can talk, regardless of what's built on top.

assets.alt: HTTP client sending a request and server sending a response

slides.markdown:
Every request has four parts: a **method** (`GET`, `POST`...), a **path** (`/users/42`), **headers** (metadata like `Host`, `Authorization`), and an optional **body** (data being sent, common on `POST`/`PUT`).

![HTTP request structure: method, path, headers, body](assets/http-request-anatomy.svg)

`GET https://api.example.com/users/42` with header `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and no body is a complete, valid request — the method and path alone say *what* you want; headers say *how* to handle it.

assets.alt: HTTP request structure: method, path, headers, body

slides.markdown:
A response mirrors the request's shape: a **status line** (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK`), **headers** (`Content-Type`, `Content-Length`), and a **body** (the actual payload — HTML, JSON, an image).

The status line's three-digit code is the first thing any client checks before even looking at the body — it's the protocol-level verdict on what happened.

| Method | Purpose | Idempotent? |
|---|---|---|
| GET | Read a resource | Yes |
| POST | Create / trigger an action | No |
| PUT | Replace a resource entirely | Yes |
| PATCH | Partially update a resource | Not guaranteed |
| DELETE | Remove a resource | Yes |

**Idempotent** means calling it once has the same end-state as calling it many times. Retrying a failed `PUT` is safe; blindly retrying a failed `POST` (say, "charge card") can double-charge — this is exactly why idempotency matters for retry logic.

Codes are grouped by their leading digit, and the family alone tells you the category of outcome before reading anything else:

- **2xx** — success (`200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`).
- **3xx** — redirection (`301 Moved Permanently`, `304 Not Modified`).
- **4xx** — client error (`400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `404 Not Found`).
- **5xx** — server error (`500 Internal Server Error`, `503 Service Unavailable`).

A client can build correct general-purpose behavior (retry on 5xx, don't retry on 4xx, follow 3xx) just from the family, without knowing the exact code.

slides.sectionTitle: Statelessness and how apps work around it
slides.markdown:
HTTP itself has **no memory** — each request is independent; the server doesn't inherently know request #2 came from the same client as request #1. That's a deliberate simplicity trade-off, not an oversight.

Since real apps need to recognize "this is the same logged-in user," they layer state on top: a `Set-Cookie` header hands the client a session ID, which it then sends back on every future request, letting the server look up state it stored server-side. HTTP stays stateless; the *application* fakes state on top.

A short list worth knowing cold:

- **`Content-Type`** — tells the receiver how to parse the body (`application/json`, `text/html`).
- **`Cache-Control`** — how long, and whether, a response can be cached.
- **`ETag`** — a fingerprint of the resource, used to check "has this changed?" without re-downloading it.
- **`Authorization`** — credentials for the request (`Bearer <token>`, `Basic <base64>`).

Get `Content-Type` wrong and a perfectly valid JSON body can get parsed as plain text — a surprisingly common real bug.

| | HTTP/1.0 | HTTP/1.1 |
|---|---|---|
| Connections | New TCP connection per request by default | Persistent ("keep-alive") by default |
| Transfer | Content-Length must be known upfront | Chunked transfer — stream without knowing total size |
| Overhead | High — handshake per request | Much lower — connection reused |

HTTP/1.1's persistent connections were the single biggest real-world performance win — skipping a fresh TCP (and often TLS) handshake for every single resource on a page.

Once a TCP connection is up: client sends `GET /page HTTP/1.1` with headers, server processes it and replies `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` with headers and the HTML body. With keep-alive, the *same* connection then carries the next request for a CSS file, an image, and so on.

![Full HTTP request/response cycle over a persistent connection](assets/http-full-cycle.svg)

This reuse is why a slow first request (cold TCP+TLS) is often followed by much faster subsequent ones on the same page load.

assets.alt: Full HTTP request/response cycle over a persistent connection

slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "As long as I return status 200, the response is fine — the details can go in the body."

**Why it's wrong:** returning `200 OK` with an error buried in the JSON body breaks every layer that inspects status codes — caches, monitoring, health checks, and API error handling all trust the status line first.

**Correct model:** use the code that matches reality. And know the difference: **401 Unauthorized** means "I don't know who you are" (missing/invalid credentials); **403 Forbidden** means "I know who you are, and you're not allowed" — a very commonly confused pair.
